item.title: On Air: Dramatic Analyst on What's New in Data
item.description: Metric trees, experimentation culture, and... AI
item.dc:creator: Elena Dyachkova
item.content:encoded:
Quick update while I’m mentally writing a proper new post (coming next week - going to be airing some grievances, stay tuned), I had a chance to appear on John Kutay’s (of Striim’s fame) podcast What’s New In Data.

Here is the link. It came out pretty short and sweet - give it a listen.

We touched upon a number of foundational topics:

  • What is product analytics, and how to connect the dots between product and business (did someone say ‘metric trees’?)

  • When to start A/B testing, and how to apply experimentation mindset if you’re not in a place to A/B test

  • Using AI in your day-to-day as a data person (text-to-sql really ain’t it for me) and how to do it productively without turning it into a crutch.

Hope you enjoy it and see you next week!

Thanks for tuning in! Subscribe not to miss next week’s post!

item.title: The Ring of Hire - Part 3: The Final Boss
item.description: Wrapping this blog series feels like wrapping up a long interview loop! Today, I discuss its squishiest parts - case and behavioral questions - and give some tips on how to ace them.
item.dc:creator: Elena Dyachkova
item.content:encoded:
First, what do I mean by case questions vs behavioral questions? Case questions include a description of a real or hypothetical situation and and a prompt to solve the problem at hand. Behavioral questions are those that start with ‘tell me about a time…’ Both types can be scattered across all rounds of the interview process, from the initial hiring manager screen all the way to the very final rounds (I tackled common loop structures in my first post of the series).

Case-Based Questions

Case questions’ usual placement in the interview process is two-fold - a manager screen can include a case, and the ‘onsite’ will definitely include a case or two, likely in stakeholder interviews. These questions tend to lean semi-technical - not technical to the point of writing code or doing some stats/calculations on the fly, but involving some specific theoretical knowledge - standard metrics or frameworks, statistical heuristics, and so on. 

For product-focused data roles, the common knowledge areas that are tested in case questions are:

  • Most common business and product metrics (including user funnel/customer journey definition in metric terms, like ‘a-ha moment’, retention metric definition, and so on)

  • Metric definition techniques (or the flip side of it - root causing a metric movement, which involves decomposing a metric)

  • A/B test design

Did someone say ‘metric trees’?

To make it more specific, I’ll share a case variations of which I’d given in dozens of interviews, and have found helpful in evaluating both the ability to think logically about business <> product metric relationships and product sense - ability to reflect on the product strategy and user experience.

I would generally use a well-known product, something like Netflix. In the setup part, I will describe what product does, identify a stakeholder and a business model. For example:

‘Let’s imagine that we work at Netflix. [here is what the product does and how]. The business model is subscription-based - all users have to have a monthly subscription to access content. The key business metric thus is the subscription revenue, and the goal for the year is to grow it by X%. You are working with the Chief Product Officer that needs helping setting up a dashboard with a set of metrics that would help them gauge how their department is contributing to keeping business on track’.

Then I would ask the candidate about how they would approach tackling this request and what would be some metrics they would consider including on the dashboard. And I’d clarify that there is no right/wrong answer and their thought process is what I’m after.

An ideal response from a senior candidate would address both the ‘how’ and the ‘what’. The ‘how’ part would include some high-level points on clarifying the end user and the use case/frequency of use, etc. for the dashboard with the fictional CPO, the process for getting feedback, as well as potentially some specifics on analytical techniques used to verify specific metric formulation - once the candidate gets into the metrics part of the answer.

The ‘what’ part is more important for me though. Generally, I’m looking for two things. Firstly, decomposing the business metric and acknowledging that we will need to look both at acquisition metrics (more new subscribers -> revenue growth) and retention metrics (higher retention at the same acquisition rate -> revenue growth). Acquisition is more or less a funnel (discovering Netflix app or website -> signing up -> early engagement/activation). Subscription retention is a little bit more tricky, because here we need to make a logical jump to ‘engaged’ retention - i.e. thinking about what a repeat engagement with the product would look like to indicate strong subscription retention.

And here comes the second thing I’m looking for - taking a beat to think (or ask questions about) product strategy and user experience.

Generally, if a candidate goes from ‘subscription retention’ to ‘repeat engagement’ right away, it is already a promising sign. If they independently clarify what that exactly can look like in a metric (e.g # users watching something at least weekly) - rather than me having to ask a bunch of follow up questions about ‘what do you mean by using the product? Opening the app or starting a movie or finishing a movie?’ - that’s a great sign. 

But an excellent (senior) candidate would also reflect on why they were prompted for ‘Netflix’ rather than, for example, ‘Hulu’. Maybe something around personalization and consuming original content? They’d also reflect on user experience - what could make a user stick with a service like this? Variety of content? Having binge-able content? Maybe that warrants metrics around watch time rather than frequency of usage? Conversion from looking for something to watch to finishing a piece of content? Average # genres engaged per month?

Again, I am not necessarily interested in the specifics of metrics themselves - I don’t work at Netflix so I don’t know what they actually measure - but the ability to empathize with the user and qualitatively frame metrics that are relevant to the product team with that in mind. I also don’t expect the candidates to know everything about Netflix - so I do try to give a good description of the product in the intro, ask them if they are familiar with it (to baseline myself) and expect them to ask follow up questions.

Another note here that when talking about introducing an ‘a-ha moment’ metric it could be worth either addressing the general heuristics explicitly or to ask the interviewer whether you should address it. Same for picking a proxy engagement metric for subscription retention in a subscription-based model.

Generally, the main places this interview goes wrong are:

  • the candidate only tacking acquisition/funnel metrics and completely overlooking retention (or vice versa)

  • struggling to go from subscription retention to engaged retention

  • not having any structure to their answer whatsoever

Another tip here is that it is not guaranteed but likely that a case like this would use a product with a similar revenue model to the company you are interviewing with. So try to refresh key metric definitions and relevant concepts ahead of time. For a SaaS company interview, read up on things like MRR, retention, upsell. For a marketplace - on GMV, marketplace liquidity and so on.

A different type of a metrics-related (somewhat?) question that I have also encountered in a couple of places was focused more on the skill of execution. The scenario would be set up something like this:

“Imagine that you come to work one day and see on the dashboard that the metric X doubled compared to the previous day. How would you figure out what is going on?”

Generally, what the interviewer will be looking for here is the logical sequence of events and a signal that the candidate can leverage appropriate resources (documentation, teammates) rather than going into deep rabbit holes. The exact response would vary depending on the metric in question and where the role sits in the data stack (a more engineering-focused role would likely have higher expectations around addressing specifics of the data pipeline and all the specific ways it can fail). '

Quick pointers on this one:

  • One of the first considerations is whether the metric movement in question looks more like a bug or a real movement (e.g. based on historical data) which would determine which investigation route you would go next

  • If it looks like a bug, the bug can be in the BI tool logic, in the data pipeline/ETL logic, or at the source, so you’d want to address all of those. Don’t forget that for ETL bugs (or BI tool bugs if we’re working with Looker) the first step should be looking at the pull request history to see if someone merged a change that can affect this metric. 

  • If it looks real - then you’d want to think more carefully about the metric in question - if it is a ratio or another calculation - which component spiked? And think about possible cases of spikes: internal changes like feature launches, marketing campaigns, or external changes - something went viral, or the company was mentioned in the news. 

    Thanks for reading Dramatic Analyst! Subscribe not to miss the next post.

MDE: Most Desirable Employee, am I right?

Another common case is an A/B test design. It usually starts with a prompt around a specific product change the team is trying to introduce, and the candidate needs to design the experiment - define the metrics and describe the process for how they would define the test duration (not necessarily doing actual calculations since that would require specific data points).

Quick pointers on what important points you are expected to touch on:

  • For metrics - you need to make sure there is a business metric in play (the reason something is tested is usually to improve conversion to payment, reduce churn and so on). In some cases, you can use that metric directly as the key experiment metric - for example, conversion from free trial to paid if the free trial is reasonably short, or conversion to purchase for e-commerce products. But the business impact may be far away from the experiment experience (often the case with retention-focused tests or conversion tests for freemium products), so you would need to state a different experiment metric that can be measured somewhat more immediately. 

  • Usually, you will also need to come up with a guardrail metric - any test has specific risks involved, so we have to measure them. If you are improving one part of the funnel, the next part can deteriorate. If you are making it easier to purchase - more users may want to return the order. If you are introducing some new tech, it could come with bugs or unintended behaviors (AI is a good example here - it can hallucinate or break if you run our of OpenAI credits or OpenAI is experiencing a service deterioration). Don’t forget to mention this!

  • When describing test design, you will need to touch on the experiment entry point (usually right before the change in the experience manifests in the UI), randomization unit (usually per user - but if it is an under-the-hood change, like an ML model change - it could be per session or per page view), and the heuristics for the test duration. Test duration in a frequentist approach is largely a function of the minimum detectable effect (MDE) (at least, if you baseline and the traffic are a given from the case setup and if you stick with 80% power and 95% confidence). It is worth explicitly addressing the heuristics of MDE definition - which is easier said that done! I usually want a stellar candidate to mention that they would look at how much the metric moved with previous experiments to get a sense for whether it is easy to move, that they would consider whether the change feels more like an incremental change or a big swing, and that they would consider ‘practical significance’ - i.e. whether moving the metric by 1 percentage point would come with a significant business upside.

  • If the case has a product with network dynamics - like a marketplace or a social network - this may be a trap! Testing in these products is not so straightforward. 50/50 randomization-based A/B testing of a new social feature in a product can be poor from the UX perspective - because half of the user-base won’t have it, so it would cause confusion and lower usability. In a marketplace, making it easier for 50% users to buy or book a unit of supply reduces availability for the control group, which would deteriorate their experience for the control group. Dealing with these scenarios in analysis, as you know, is tricky, so I doubt that you would be required to go in depth, but just noting some possible approaches like geographical clustering (or similar) could be enough. 

Some common A/B test scenarios I’ve encountered in interviews:

  • In subscription or SaaS products - changing various free trial dynamics (testing a longer trial length, asking or not asking for a credit card upfront, testing a freemium offering, moving the paywall around in the onboarding flow)

  • In marketplaces - making listings better (better photos, descriptions, introducing social proof - like ratings - for sellers), making the browsing experience better (sorting/ranking improvements, adding chatbot to help find the right item), or making more money by adding or favoring ‘sponsored’ listings in the browsing experience

  • In consumer products - introducing new features with a goal of reducing churn (e.g. introducing a social feature, introducing gamification components - badges, streaks)

Tell me about your past project…

It is not uncommon to be asked, usually at earlier interview stages, to walk the interviewer through one of your past projects. How to approach this prompt?

First of all, be prepared for it - before the interview think about a past project that aligns with what the role is looking for. If it is a manager role, think about a project where you elevated your team or successfully brought multiple people together. If it is a role on a growth team, think about something related to experimentation and/or with immediate monetary impact.

Secondly, don’t jump straight into what you did step by step. Frame the context around ‘why’ - why did you embark on this project, what was the problem you were solving, what goal did you have? As you are conveying this, remember that your interviewer may not be intimately familiar with your company or product, so it could help to give a little context that is pertinent (what’s the business model, what is the key value prop).

And after describing the specifics of the project - circle back to the ‘why’ - did it pan out as expected? What was the impact?

It can be tricky to balance the right level of technical detail for laying out the specifics of the project. If you over-explain, you can sound patronizing. If you bombard a non-technical person with too much technical detail, they will think you don’t know how to convey your thoughts clearly. So definitely make sure you understand the type of person you are talking to - a business stakeholder or a manager who will be more interested in impact - vs someone who is more interested in going into detail. And you can also explicitly ask what to focus on and whether to go into technical detail for specific phases of the project. 

One of my pet peeves is when in this prompt (and probably other behavioral prompts) the candidate speaks about what ‘we’ did the entire time. There can be so many reasons why they would do that - it was truly a team effort they participated in, it was their effort but they don’t like to boast, it was a team effort that they didn’t participate in but want the credit? I wouldn’t want to hire the latter candidate. I would hire the first two, but I’d still want to know what is it that they did vs. their teammates, so please be more specific to avoid getting disqualified in fear that you are the freeloader of the project that is trying to hide that fact. 

And expect that you will get a question along the lines of: ‘if you could redo it, what would you do differently?’, or ‘can you reflect on what could have gone better?’, so be ready with an answer that doesn’t sound like finger pointing. Making mistakes is a good thing. I liked how Carole Robin framed mistakes as AFOG - another effing opportunity for growth. So speak honestly about your mistakes AND how you carried your learnings forward. 

Tell me about a time when…

If you want to figure out what type of behavioral questions you may get asked at a given company, here’s a tip. Google ‘CompanyName values’ - read through their values page. Do any of these values get mentioned in the job description in a way? Then take those values and google ‘ValueName interview behavioral questions’ - you will likely find a list that would be fairly representative of what to expect, so you can prep your answers.

Generally, the advice is to use a STAR framework (Situation-Task-Action-Result) for answering them - which I think is a solid advice. There are a lot of good articles about this framework, for example, this one.

Usually, the value-based behavioral questions will be somewhat tailored to the role as well. Some common questions that come up in data interviews are the following:

  • Tell me about a time when you made a mistake…

  • Tell me about a time when you disagreed with a stakeholder’s decision.. (we have to acknowledge that the data is not end all be all, so stakeholders can be drawing on other valid sources of information or experiences, and they can be wrong too but we can also show them why with data - retroactively)

  • Tell me about a time when you invited an opposing opinion / invited a collaborator with a different perspective.. (all data folks should have good examples here about collaborating with qualitative research folks and with your stakeholders)

  • Tell me about a time when you had to make a decision without sufficient data / with messy data… (we all have to navigate precision/speed tradeoffs)

Closing notes

Hopefully this three-part series was helpful for the folks going through interviewing at the moment, as well as for hiring managers wanting to spruce up their interview loops.

The final note I’ll give is that interviewing gets easier with practice - so I generally encourage everyone to interview at least once in a while, even if you’re not actively looking. This way you stay abreast of what skills are in demand, how hard it is to meet hiring bars, how much money you can pull. And if you don’t pass an interview - do ask for feedback. A lot of companies wouldn’t give feedback or would give very canned responses (in fear of potential legal consequences) but if you have a good recruiter and/or hiring manager, and especially if you’ve gotten far into the loop, they would likely be willing to jump on a call to give you a TLDR. Doesn’t hurt to ask!

And please let me know in the comments if you can use some help with hiring or interviewing strategy or if you have good examples of common cases and behavioral questions you’ve encountered as a candidate!

Thanks for reading Dramatic Analyst! Subscribe to make sure you don’t miss future posts!

item.title: The Ring of Hire, pt. 2. The Battle of the Resumes...
item.description: ...or some practical tips for crafting a good resume and passing the initial technical screen for product analytics or generalist analytics/data science roles.
item.dc:creator: Elena Dyachkova
item.content:encoded:
In my previous post, I covered the hiring manager point of view - how do I approach designing hiring loops for analytics roles. Today, I want to tap into the candidate view and provide some practical advice for the initial stages of the job application and interview process - the resume submission, and the initial technical screen. In the next and last part of this series, I will tackle case study and behavioral interviews.

Job market in 2024 remains challenging. Judging by layoffs.fyi data, there is still hundreds if not thousands of folks in tech alone laid off every week. At the same time, there are still lots of open roles. I’m looking out for roles for some former teammates, and I’m seeing interesting things pop up across Linkedin, outerjoin, various data-focused slack communities daily (for what it’s worth, it feels like currently data engineers and marketing analysts are more in demand relative to 2021-2022, so if I was giving advice on where to uplevel - there!). But, of course, things are very competitive.

I’ve experienced it myself, where in 2021 I was getting lots of interviews, hiring processes were moving quickly, I was getting almost no rejections. In 2022, there were definitely more of resumes going into the void, and I got a couple of rejections that quite frankly stung, as they felt a bit (or a lot) nit-picky. In total, I got rejected from ClassDojo, IBM, NFL, Grindr, Pave, Zocdoc, Spotify, ClickUp, OneMedical, Faire at various stages and for various reasons, a couple of them I totally bombed myself - it happens - but I also got three great offers.

Now that I’ve got to marinate on all this copious interviewing, I’m compiling some practical advice below. Disclaimer: of course, not every hiring manager thinks and evaluates like me, so your mileage might vary.

Resume tips

In the last couple of weeks, there were two interesting threads on Twitter on this very topic. 

In one of them, someone shared a fake resume with a funny/obscene name that consisted of lots of numbers-focused bullet points, some of which contained references to “increasing average coffee break time” and other deeply unserious things. This resume reportedly secured the author several dozen interviews at places like Databricks, MongoDB, among others. The point they were trying to make was that resumes get screened fast, so you’ve got to frame each bullet point with numbers. 

I think they failed to make the point fully, given that their resume had role-fitting titles and exclusively FAANG employers which.. duh.. will get you screened no matter what is in the bullet points. But they were also not wrong that resumes get screened quickly, and people like when candidates drive outcomes rather than outputs.

I’m not a huge stickler for numbers specifically, I’m sure most of the ‘increased revenue by X%’ statements especially in roles like data, product (rather than e.g. sales) are between completely made up to aspirational, but I do look for the bullets to be framed something like: ‘Discovered opportunity -> highlighted opportunity -> helped improve X’ or ‘Discovered opportunity -> developed solution -> made a difference’. 

For example: ‘Reduced pipeline failures by implementing unit testing framework’ or ‘Designed a geo-based incrementality test for paid marketing that discovered inefficiencies in media spend and helped target the budget towards higher-performing channels’. 

Bullets generally shouldn’t be a listing of all the job duties (if you are a product analyst, I would expect that you evaluate A/B tests and feature launches) or focus on vanity metrics like ‘built 1000 dashboards’ or ‘developed 50 KPIs’. If anything, the latter is a bit of a red flag - how many of these dashboards or KPIs are actually in productive use?

Another thread reasoned that (probably, especially with AI making it easier) both the candidates are super-tailoring resumes for very specific technical requirements, and recruiters are screening for the same which leads to sub-optimal outcomes.

It is an interesting idea to do this sort of an anti-filtering as a hiring manager: ask for a very specific technology, like some very niche vendor and then filter OUT resumes that highlighted it assuming they just copy-pasted the requirements without much thought. Next time I’m hiring, I might pay more attention to that!

In the product analytics realm, the requirements are generally not super specific when it comes to technologies (yes, you absolutely should know SQL and something about event data and experimentation, but whether you used Segment or Rudderstack, Amplitude or Mixpanel, is largely irrelevant). But I imagine, it is not quite the same on the data engineering or ML side of things.

Anyways, here is how I scan resumes and some brief tips:

  • First, I check general career alignment - titles and years of experience, this already filters a lot of folks, no surprise in this environment but lots of folks ‘spray and pray’! If the alignment is not evident but you believe you are still a great fit (e.g. you’re applying for an IC role after being in senior leadership for 5 years, or you’ve transitioned to product management in the last few years but want to get back into data) and are intentional about your application, a very short cover letter may be helpful.

  • Then, I start reading the bullet points from the most recent job - looking for the evidence of problem solving, being able to explain the ‘why’ behind activities; here I will also be looking for specific experiences required in the job description - e.g. I may need someone who is already hands on with experimentation - I’d want that mentioned explicitly. For people managers, I’d look at some reference to improving team efficiency, helping up-level teammates, developing processes or best practices.

  • Depending on the time at the last job and whether I’m seeing the alignment, I may look at the previous jobs, too.

I do like to read all resumes myself (vs outsourcing it all to the recruiter), but that does mean that I’m going through them quickly. So I do see value in clean organization, bolding key words in each bullet, making sure that it is easy to visually grasp previous titles and years worked. But I generally do not look at education at all, unless it is an internship or very junior position where I would look at the major (but not the school or the GPA).

And do try to keep it to a couple of pages tops!

When it comes to customizing resumes for each role - I personally do not advise that, but again, your mileage may vary. I think that customizing for each job is very time consuming and that time can be better spent trying to get connections or informational interviews at these companies. I usually have a couple of generic resume versions (e.g. in my case it would be a ‘manager’ flavor resume, and an ‘IC’ flavor resume), and I would only customize for a few jobs that I’d consider absolute dream opportunities. 

Technical Screen

For product analytics or adjacent roles, by and large, the initial technical screen is SQL (live or as a take-home exercise) and I’ve seen it be one of two flavors:

  • You are given some data that you need to wrangle. Could be actual data loaded in a collaborative environment like Hackerrank or a notebook like Hex or Deepnote, or just descriptions of tables/columns - where you can write the code but can’t run it.

  • Or, you need to first define a data warehouse design, and then write SQL off of the schema you designed.

    Thanks for reading Dramatic Analyst! Subscribe not to miss the next post!

The general SQL manipulation is usually very similar across both cases:

  • You need to be able to summarize a table (COUNT, SUM, AVG functions; don’t forget your group bys!) - usually a plain aggregation and a conditional one: COUNT(distinct CASE WHEN country = ‘US’ THEN user_id END) - make sure you know where the ‘distinct’ goes relative to ‘case when’ and don’t forget the ‘end’! 

  • You need to join two tables (and then summarize), so make sure you understand the left and inner join syntax.

    • A pretty common pattern here, especially for product analytics, is to calculate some conversion rate (from signup to subscription, from exposure to an A/B test to the successful outcome) by joining the ‘event’ (really, a timestamp) of completing the funnel for each ‘user’ or ‘customer’ object, and then summarize how many users did have a non-null timestamp, or a non-null timestamp within X days or hours from the funnel entry. Here you’ll get a join, an aggregation, a conditional, and some ‘datediff’ or ‘dateadd’ to boot.

    • Strangely, there is a lot of terrible advice on funnel SQL online. After doing a cursory search for this blog, I was sad to find that majority of resources just have you counting users who reached each funnel stage in the same period and doing divison - which isn’t really a conversion rate since you are not looking at the same population of users at each stage. This article outlines cleaner approaches (for a SQL screen I would go with the one titled ‘the good’.

  • Less common, but you may encounter some window functions, too. Usually, rank() or row_number() (do you know the difference?)

There are some great resources online that will help you practice. I really like this quick free tutorial from Mode as it is built with very common and practical use cases and it covers all the bases. As long as you can confidently do all the manipulations described there on your own, you should be a-ok. Another place to practice is W3schools, and of course there are paid resources too - like Datacamp, InterviewQuery, Leetcode.

However, even if you are great with SQL, coding live can be a completely different beast from doing it as a take home, so here are some tips:

  • Treat the interview as a collaborative conversation. Before jumping into coding something up, verbalize your thought process to the interviewer. That way, if you made a typo, the interviewer would know it for what it is, since they would have already heard that your logic was correct.

  • In the same vein, clarify your assumptions. For example, in most cases, these interviews aren’t checking for ability to write a super-optimized code, but it doesn’t hurt to clarify: ‘Do you want me to take into consideration the possibility of handling a really large dataset?’ or ‘Do I need to optimize for quick runtime?’. 

  • Make your code easily debuggable for your own sake. If you’re writing a join, alias them tables. If you’re trying to do multiple joins and an aggregation in one query - don’t. Write CTEs (common table expressions), so much more readable and easier to troubleshoot step by step.

  • Unless explicitly stated, don’t assume that the data you’re given is sanitized. Ask or check for quirks in the data - most common one being duplicates. If you’re asked to join a couple of tables to calculate a conversion rate, can a user be at a given stage of the funnel twice? Can they reach the second stage of the funnel while bypassing the initial stage? Some interviewers will tell you - ‘it’s fine, assume the data is clean’, some interviewers expect you to know the edge cases and will decline you for not clarifying those assumptions.

  • If you forgot a thing (cough cough window function syntax cough cough), say so and ask if it’s ok to Google it real quick, most normal data people google date/time conversions every week, so I bet you would be allowed to look something up.

  • Don’t get flustered with typos or SQL flavor-related things (did I just say date/time conversions again?), everyone makes typos, and nobody knows all SQL flavors off the top of their heads. However, if you are doing a SQL screen as a take-home, then expect to need to deliver much more precision!

In the case where you need to define the schema first, the setup can be something along the lines of: ‘Imagine that you are building an e-commerce app that serves X purpose and has Y business model, how would you set up the data structure to ensure that it fulfills the use case?’. For these prompts, you’d want to know a little bit of Kimball foundations - you need a table per each key business object (e.g. seller, customer, product) and a table for key activities that the customers undertake and that drive revenue. In this case it would be orders (or some combination of orders, deliveries, restocks). 

There is generally not a single right or wrong answer, but a good answer would:

  • Make sure that you are accounting for everything that was given to you in the prompt. E.g. if your prompt is that this e-commerce product suggests all sellers within walkable distance from the customer, you probably would want to make sure you are capturing location data for customers and sellers in your data model. If your prompt describes a SaaS product, you would want to make sure that you are capturing subscriptions and subscription statuses in some way.

  • Take into account the user experience of the target product. What information about an item would a user want to see on the e-commerce website? Brand? Price? Rating? Make sure to talk through it and include all the relevant columns into the table.

  • Don’t be afraid to clarify any assumptions, the most important one being - are we building the data model for the backend of the product, or for the analytics use cases? In the latter case, you’d want to focus more on helpful aggregations for calculating business metrics, while in the former case, you’d want to focus on structuring the data so that the application can easily ‘fetch’ the elements of user experience.

  • Don’t spend too much time on esoteric things. For example, if while discussing how to capture the location of your e-commerce store, you have spent five minutes debating whether you need longitude and latitude, you probably are going astray (unless you are interviewing for a location tracking company). Instead ask - ‘would it be ok to use zip code for simplicity, or do I need to go into more depth?’

Verbalize, verbalize, verbalize. Verbalize assumptions, verbalize your logic before coding, verbalize if you have questions. And keep it simple!

I have encountered only a few technical screens for Senior/Staff product analytics roles with more complexity than described above, for example:

  • Numpy/pandas-focused python to calculate A/B test results (sans stats). Need to know how to filter, group by, and aggregate a dataframe

  • Vanilla python - write a simple function. Need to know how to define a function, and how to write a loop. (I had this task during an Instacart screen some years ago - had to write a function for a factorial, I totally didn’t do it but still passed the overall interview on the account of my snappyl SQL)

  • Regex in a SQL query. This one was in a take-home, which is less threatening as I could Google it. I would have probably panicked if that happened during a live test.

Hopefully, with the tips above you feel a little more prepared (or at least know what to work on to feel more prepared!). In my next blogpost (in ~2-3 weeks) I will tackle the other parts of the interviewing process - the hiring manager interview, the case-based interviews, and common behavioral questions for data people. I will share my favorite questions and cases and tips on how to effectively tackle them.

item.title: The Ring of Hire. Part 1.
item.description: When I was starting to dip my toes into people management, I dreaded hiring! Now, it is one of my favorite parts of the job. Here is how I go about finding new teammates. No resume roasting included..
item.dc:creator: Elena Dyachkova
item.content:encoded:
I am very introverted, very indecisive, and I am not a native English speaker… Put all of that together, and here I was sweating bullets before interviewing someone on the phone (pre-pandemic), worrying that I won’t understand their English without being able to see them, and that I might have to reject them even if they are great but not meeting requirements for the job. I was a nervous wreck!

COVID took care of the phone interviews, I’ve done lots of interviewing and hiring manager training at Peloton, got lots of practice reps under my belt, but what really changed my outlook was a single conversation. I got connected with someone junior at the time that I wasn’t hiring. It was an informational interview, still, but I didn’t have a script and a scorecard, and the conversation was just… flowing. I got to learn so much about the person in front of me without having all the worry and the pressure I was putting on myself. 

At that moment I realized that I was doing everything by the book but missing out on the opportunity to be curious and really get to know the person in front of me. After this light-bulb moment, I cherish every opportunity to connect with a candidate, and this shapes my approach to designing and conducting interview loops. 

In the first part of my Ring of Hire series, I will share my guiding principles for organizing a hiring process for data roles - hope it helps some new hiring managers get started - and some candidates to see behind the scenes to prepare for their interviews. In the second part (in ~2 weeks), I will share a few specific questions and cases that I like to ask.

Note that I have mostly hired for product analytics/product data science or adjacent roles, so not everything may be applicable to roles in the Data Engineering or ML realm! I am currently hiring for a Data Engineer role for the first time, and trust me, I had to lean on my gracious peers from the data community and hire a consultant to help button up the technical interview outlines and conduct some interviews!

Here are, in brief, the few principles that underpin my hiring philosophy:

  • Be very clear about screening and scoring focus for each interview and interviewer: cover all the bases, don’t duplicate, ensure consistency across candidates

  • Meet with the panel to talk through the role and the process, get a lot of feedback

  • Don’t outsource resume screening to ATS

  • Meet the candidate early, get to know what drives them, describe your vision of the role in a way that resonates

  • Make the process equitable

  • Don’t give nightmare take-homes or live coding screens: take homes should be short and sweet, live coding sessions - open book, collaborative, reminiscent of real workflows

Internal process

Before diving into the specifics of the interview loop, I want to share what the prep looks like.

Of course, the first step is to get the headcount approved, which generally means that I have an idea of what the person is going to work on both in short- and in long-term. When I was just starting out as a manager, I was really afraid to ask for headcount - I knew I had a burning need (either for a skillset or for extra bandwidth), but I was worried that the person I hire will solve my problem and then will be bored, sitting without work to do…

Have you ever seen a data person without work to do? Ha ha ha. I was naive.

I read somewhere that good managers hire not for ‘now’ but for ‘three years in the future’. I think there is some truth to that. I don’t think it means that we should “always be hiring” but that it’s prudent not to over-index on specific role requirements for ‘today’ but if you’re hiring a full-time person, it is important to spend a minute thinking about their potential growth vector. And if the immediate need is overwhelming then maybe hiring a consultant or a contractor is a better move?

But I digress! Get the general idea of what the short-to-long term scope would be, pitch it by highlighting high business-impact initiatives that this role would address that would fall by wayside without the hire, hopefully get the green light.

Next step - job description! I usually do lots of research on Linkedin - compiling parts of job descriptions that resonate before weaving them into a cohesive outline with the specifics sprinkled in. Now that lots of companies publish salary ranges, I also compile benchmarks for my HR partners during the same step. In the job description, I try to clearly state requirements and nice-to-haves, as well as highlight specifics of the day-to-day (‘In this role you will…’).

Once the job description is done, I write up a loop, tagging in specific folks that I want to participate in the process. For every step of the loop, from resume screen to each interview, I write out very specifically what the focus area is: some interviews will be purely technical (coding, statistics), some will be semi-technical (product cases), and some - purely behavioral. It may be harder to pin down specifics ‘skills’ the less technical the interview is, but the entire loop should covers all the bases, so to speak, in the most efficient way - without much overlap or duplication, and each interviewer has to understand what exactly they are grading candidates on (not on the ‘vibes’) and can apply a consistent approach to scoring.

For semi-technical and behavioral interviews, I usually go off the ‘career ladder’ for my team, screening for some key skills at an appropriate level with cases or ‘tell me about a time when’ - like handling ambiguity, synthesizing recommendations for leadership or non-technical audience, systems thinking. And I use the company values to shape behavioral questions spread out across several interviews - one value per interview. At Peloton we had a great question bank for all company values, but it is also easy to get some inspiration online (Google or ChatGPT - choose your fighter) - search for ‘behavioral interview questions for “empowerment” or whatever value you want to assess. 

Outlining clear focus areas and scoring attributes for each interviewer also gives me flexibility - if the interviewer is experienced, they usually would want to write their own script once they understand their role in the process. If they are less seasoned or very busy, I would write a version of a script for them and ask for feedback.

Once the loop is written out, I like to do an in-person kick-off, where I can describe the idea candidate more informally, talk through the scope of their role so the interviewers can envision how they would work with that person, and discuss the loop live. I also calibrate with the recruiter early and often. My current recruiting partner at Bubble, Mac, is an absolute wizard  - he asks a lot of questions which helps me clarify my thinking, and he brings lots of Linkedin profiles of potential candidates to review together and kick-off sourcing.

The Loop 

My favorite structure of the loop for a mid-level product analytics (or similar) is the following:

  1. Resume review: for the most part, I’ve been reviewing resumes myself. I’ve participated in hiring in four different companies now, and at none of them did we use some ATS matching or filtering. Hence the advice about including keywords in white font or sending your resume in a word doc so that ATS can parse it better has always been weird to me (seriously, please don’t, just PDF it, word docs appear weird in ATS systems). But it still makes sense to explicitly include some specific things that the job description is asking for - I scan resumes very fast!

  2. Recruiter screen: general experience & interest alignment, opportunity to sell the candidate on the company & where it is going, the usual HR stuff (work authorization, location, timelines, target comp if they are willing to share - we do disclose our bands, and so on)

  3. Hiring manager screen: opportunity to tell the candidate about the vision for the role in-depth and address their questions, opportunity to get to know them better - what motivates them, what are the highlights and lowlights of their week, what are some things that they are excited about learning. On the more technical side of things, I don’t usually go for any coding or stats in this interview, instead I give a product analytics/systems thinking case - for example, trying to conceptualize a metrics framework for a well-known product. 

It is pretty interesting that different interviews approach the ‘order’ of hiring manager interview differently - at places like Facebook, Instacart, and even at some smaller companies, it is not uncommon for the first real interview to be a technical screen with a peer/teammate. It is definitely more efficient for the hiring manager - less candidates make it to them, but I feel like this is not a great candidate experience, as a candidate I’d want to meet a hiring manager as early as possible so I can get a better feel for the role. And I also feel like I can filter folks pretty well on ‘motivation’ and product sense early on so I don’t have to subject them to a live coding session or a take-home if it’s not a fit. For example, if I’m operating on a small team, I need someone who is very impact-driven, it is pretty easy to tell from a conversation if a candidate is more craft-driven or execution-driven. Even if they are brilliant, that’s not going to work.

  1. Technical screen: I have varied my approach to this one depending on the needs of the role - I’ve done both live screens and take-homes. I think neither of them are exactly ‘equitable’. Some people are bad at live coding because of the nerves or because they don’t think well on the spot, take-homes are bad for folks with families and busy jobs, so it is really hard to make everyone 100% happy, but there are some mitigations. Take-homes should be well-defined and reasonable to complete in 1-2 hours (and give candidates enough time to tackle it - at least a week). Live coding should be open-book and collaborative with the interviewer to simulate real work environment - we all google stuff. But generally, in roles with more ‘coding’ - i.e. when a product analyst will be contributing to the analytics engineering body of work, a live coding session may be more efficient in testing for that. Otherwise, I like a light take home to test for the ability to synthesize information clearly and frame a cohesive story.

My absolute worst take home as a candidate was that from Spotify. It seems that they give the same one for all data science roles across their music, ads, podcasts, audiobooks teams - a huge ‘playlist’ dataset with dozens and dozens of features and a vague prompt along the lines of ‘figure out what a good playlist is from this dataset’. I was interviewing for an ads team, so I tried to spin it from that perspective (looking at reach/frequency metrics - to see which playlists are the best for advertisers) but I’m pretty sure I spectacularly bombed it after a sleepless night trying to make some decision tree models work.

  1. Virtual onsite: 

    1. Teammate interview: chance to double-click on some technical aspects in more depth (e.g. statistics, experimentation, working with event-like data for product analytics) and assess how the person collaborates, how they can contribute to the team improvement

    2. Cross-functional partner interview: usually an end-to-end case with the product manager (A/B test or a feature launch) and assess how the candidate conveys information to non-technical audience, how they’ve handled decision-making with limited information and disagreements in the past.

    3. For more senior roles, there may be another cross-functional partner in play - an engineering leader, or a growth/marketing partner

    4. Skip-level interview, that is usually more behavioral/values alignment-focused, and double-clicks on any remaining questions or concerns from previous interviews

Equitable practices

It is no secret that the data field is not all that diverse, so is tech overall. Very male-dominated, very underrepresented when it comes to Black and Latino folks, not always friendly for caregivers or older folks, the more ‘technical’ and the more senior the role - the worse. The best remedy is to not just hire equitably, but to also do a lot of internships and hire juniors, but understandably in the current capital climate this may be tougher (junior folks need a lot of mentorship, and with leaner teams that becomes more of a challenge). So at the very least, do your best with some best practices:

  • Source! Reach out to folks you know to see if they have good candidates that are looking, reach out to professional communities (e.g. Data Angels, Women in Product, Moms in Tech, Black Women in Data)

  • While it is not worth robotically reading the interview scripts verbatim, it is a good practice to ensure all candidates get similar sets of core questions in a similar order and are graded on same attributes

  • Don’t compare candidates to one another - compare them to the requirements of the role

  • Don’t read other people’s scorecards before filling yours out

  • Fill out your scorecard right after the interview before you forget the specifics and biases creep in, take notes during the interview

  • Don’t ask personal questions - I wouldn’t even ask anything about which school they went to, when they graduated, where they’re from, and so on

  • I try to also consciously think about the combination of backgrounds I have on the team to make sure it is well rounded. If everyone on the team is ex-FAANG then the team will probably have a bunch of blind spots when it comes to ways of working. But imagine if you have someone from big tech, someone with academic background, a jack-of-all-trades from a small startup - together you will be unstoppable!

Stay tuned…

In a couple of weeks, I will share some practical tips for all folks on the interviewing battlefield - from my perspective as a hiring manager after filling > 20 roles in the last couple of years - and as a candidate after enduring two interviewing cycles myself in the similar time span:

  • How to make your resume stand out

  • My favorite product cases and what I look for in responses

  • Common patterns for SQL screens

item.title: What I learned and didn't learn from the "bible" of A/B testing...
item.description: Ronny Kohavi’s book is a must-read for anyone dealing with experimentation, but the ‘application’ is, unsurprisingly, messier than theory. Turns out, experimentation is also a soft skill!
item.dc:creator: Elena Dyachkova
item.content:encoded:
Even though I went to school for economics and applied math, my first exposure to A/B testing happened in 2017, when I was doing a so-called “modern” online MBA through Quantic. The material was very high-level, but it was enough for me to pass the job interview at Peloton and kick off some experiments while there.

The basic intuition that their materials captured is fairly straightforward:

  • If there is one and only one difference between two groups (which is achieved by randomly assigning users to groups and making sure the product is really introducing a single change), then we can reason about the impact of this change. Any externalities - what happened with the market, in the media, due to other departments’ launches - don’t muddle the assessment, given that they would affect both group the same

  • It is not enough to say that your metric increased in group B and didn’t increase in group A, we need to apply statistical testing to ensure that the difference you’re seeing isn’t just the product of sampling - i.e. running the test at a specific moment in time

  • If we have enough users across A and B groups and our metric is straightforward (e.g. conversion rate, which is just a representation of a binary outcome for each ‘test subject’), we can leverage an online calculator to figure out if your results are indeed statistically significant

  • It is important to figure out how big of a population your test needs upfront. And you should wait to report the results until you do have the right sample size, so you aren’t reporting an accidental fluctuation as a statistically significant result

(Of course, the points above can be a bit more statistically rigorous, and some of them can be softened e.g. if you’re Bayesian, but I’m going with the basics here, bear with me!)

If you have the above down pat, you’re already doing better than ~70% of people that do A/B testing! Congratulations!

Book Smarts…

Now it is a good time to tackle Ronny Kohavi’s book Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments that is rightfully dubbed as The Bible of the A/B testing. (I also recently learned that Ronny & his coauthors give all proceeds from the sales to charities, so it is a good purchase if the library waitlist is too long).

Thanks for reading Dramatic Analyst! Subscribe to receive new posts in your inbox!

I will confess, when I tackled this book initially, I got maybe 60% into it and ran out of gusto. It is not a dense book by any means (doesn’t feel like you’re reading an economics journal article, if you know what I mean), but it requires undivided attention. So when I joined Spring Health, we organized a book club to keep each other accountable for reading and discussing a few chapters a month.

This book is full of gems, from discussing experimentation culture, to experiment design, to technical specifics of experiment setup, to running experimentation programs at scale, and even ethics.

Here are a few things that I found the most impactful:

  1. Information about things that can (and will) go wrong and ways to get ahead of it. For example, from this book I learned about the Sample Ratio Mismatch (when you are deploying test at 50/50 but you’re seeing uneven group sizes in your analysis). Turns out, you can run a stat test to see if your difference in group sizes is big enough to be worrisome. The book also goes in detail on A/A testing - i.e. practicing an A/B test rollout (randomization & data collection) without introducing any UX changes. Highly recommend doing it if you are deploying your first A/B test or getting into some complex conditional logic for when your users need and not need to be included in the test. When we ran one of those at Spring Health, we found that our data logging was not capturing test group assignments at the right time, and our assignments weren’t sticking across mobile and web.

Another resource I like on the topic of various experimentation bugs is this 5-minute talk from NormConf

  1. This book also helped me better understand the role of ‘variance’ in the ultimate success of the test. Reducing variance improves sensitivity of the test (ability to detect the treatment effect when it exists). One of the simple ways to do it is considering whether the outcome metric can be made binary - e.g. instead of # of workouts per week on Peloton, it can be ‘did the user workout or not’ or ‘% users who worked out at least X times’ so you don’t fall victim to users who like to stack four Emma Lovewell Crush Your Classes every day.

    And more ‘fancy’ methods like CUPED are really there to reduce variance and thus enable us to make decisions quicker - i.e. with a smaller sample.

  2. Kohavi’s book has one of the best explanations of gradual ramp for experiments. Turns out, rolling an A/B test at 10% doesn’t mean that 90% of the users is control and 10% - test. It means that 10% of the users are within the test, with a 50/50 split, i.e. 5% - in test, and 5% - in control.

  3. Lastly, both in the book, and in his interview on Lenny’s podcast, Ronny mentions that the vast majority of experiments don’t show expected improvements! This is a great thing to remember when you’re in a stretch of several not ‘stat sig’ tests and your product manager starts questioning whether it is humanly possible to move the metric and whether you need a new analysis methodology.

    No kidding, I have been previously asked in an interview by a marketer: ‘If you got A/B test results that aren’t statistically significant, would you reanalyze the same test some other way to get to significance?’.

    Anyways, remember, the only ‘failed’ test is the one without learnings, and a ‘flat’ test doesn’t equal a test without learnings.

… “Street” Smarts

Reading this book feels almost like reading a textbook, it is so comprehensive, and written with so much precision. You feel more than empowered to go and run an experimentation program. But of course, the reality starts to diverge from the theory pretty quickly. The author of the book is drawing a lot on his experience at larger companies like Microsoft, Amazon, and Airbnb, and while the book covers the ‘crawl -> walk -> run’ stages of experimentation maturity, sometimes it takes some effort to get to crawling in the first place, and not even from the technical standpoint. 

When I joined my first B2B product team, after my stints doing experimentation in a B2C context, the team was hoping to launch a redesigned part of the onboarding flow as a test - their first ever. There were quite a few new customers joining soon, meaning that there would be lots of new users going through onboarding, so getting to the right sample size would be trivial.

Except… the sales team told us we couldn’t test on any customers that joined in the previous 90 days, leaving us with a much more extended timeline to reach statistical significance. In my mind, it was so odd - why not try to accelerate the path for our new users to get a better experience? Wouldn’t the customers be excited to get in on some innovation?

Turns out, I needed to learn more about the workings of this product’s sales and enablement cycles. The customers’ implementation leads were getting extensive demos of what the ‘sign up’ experience would look like for the users. Make it even subtly divergent, and if their employees (end users) get confused, it would cause lots of swirl internally, and eventually - reaching our sales and support teams.

‘But how would we run our A/B test without sufficient sample?’, we asked.

‘Can customer X be ‘A’ and customer Y be ‘B’?, the enablement team said.

‘But this is not how any of this works…’ I thought to myself, frustratedly. 

Eventually, we learned more about the risks around new customer launch, led an A/B testing ‘lunch and learn’ for the product and sales teams, and met in the middle - we were able to work with some new customers, but not others.

Unfortunately, the A/B test ended up being flat, which is a story for a another day (and another learning here is that for the first ever A/B test in the company, it is better to start with something that is more likely to be a shoo-in, to create momentum!)

Just take the MDE and just plug it into calculator!

Another thing that books and articles make sound so academic and precise, is the A/B test design.

You have the metric baseline, the historical ‘traffic’ to the experiment entry-point. You define the Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE) by looking at how much your target metric moved with the past tests or launches and combining that with ‘practical significance’. Then you use 95% confidence and 80% power (and don’t touch it, it is an industry standard! /s), plug it in the calculator… boom, here is your sample size.

In reality though, Minimum Detectable Effect is like.. Folklore.

If you haven’t experimented before on the same metric, it is really hard to assess how sensitive it would be. If the metric is fairly far from the business impact (e.g. some engagement metric that has a sufficient lag before propagating to churn rate movement), assessing practical significance also involves a bunch of assumptions… that require a few experiments each in the first place.

The way it often works in practice is you present the product manager with options: “If we run this for 4 weeks, we assess a to 5 p.p. With 95% confidence, if we want to learn faster - we can go for a larger MDE or be ok with a higher chance of a false positive.” Having this discussion in a way that your product partners aren’t feeling pelted with stats, is an art and science in itself.

Really, all it comes down to is - we need practice to figure it out. Putting some ‘reps’ under our belt when we have more questions than solution. It may take months or even years for things to really click in the way the book describes, and it can feel so frustrating that things aren’t as clear cut and scientific. But why not treat it as an experiment too? Very meta, but this approach very materially takes a lot of stress away!

Anyway, here are some reading materials…

To take it full circle… I still like reading, especially materials that have ‘case studies’ within. So of course I will share some resources if you are on a path to being a better ‘experimentator’!

  • If you want to get a cliff notes edition of Ronny’s book, hit me in the comments, I can share 23 pages of notes I compiled for our book club meeting!

  • I really like the book Statistics Done Wrong - it is written around research studies rather than product experimentation, but the stats are the same

  • If you follow some folks from Eppo on Linkedin - particularly Sven and Evan they share great recaps of their journal club pursuits and quality blog posts experimentation-related topics

  • There are some great courses out there too - Reforge’s Experimentation + Testing course and Stephanie Pancoast’s Practical A/B Testing course on Uplimit are both very high quality!

As for me, catch me at the Data Mishaps Night on March 7 talking about… data pipelines unraveling! See you then!

item.title: Call of Duty
item.description: If you are a part of a friendly data team, one day you inevitably find yourself overwhelmed with requests. Do you grumble about not being a service desk or do you capitalize on being in demand?
item.dc:creator: Elena Dyachkova
item.content:encoded:
Probably, both! Data people like to grumble in general, because we like for things to make sense, have a structured reasoning, and a degree of predictability. Naturally, that doesn’t always match our reality. But, I’ve found that over-indexing on grumbling and running a strict JIRA backlog for new requests (or refusing to take them outside of the quarterly planning) can do more harm than good in the team’s journey towards becoming a trusted and valued thought partner.

So, what do you do? Do you just deal with constantly being interrupted and context-switching and forego meaningful progress on generative work? Not at all! On-call rotation to the rescue!

Now, it can definitely use a bit of a different branding. On-call in tech has a connotation of being woken up in the middle of the night by a PagerDuty alert. If your data team is responsible for data pipelines that feed into the user-facing product in some way (especially when it comes to critical points of user experience, like the ability to perform the key action in the product, right access levels for PII, payments, and so on) - that may still be your reality. 

But for teams that are focused on analysis, reporting, research - it is really not all that scary. So if you are introducing this concept to your team, call it something different so as not to get an immediate rejection (learn from my mistakes!). At Spring Health, the data engineering team called the ‘on-call’ person ‘the sprint guardian’ which admittedly sounds much more noble.

Here is how it could work…

I first started thinking about on-call at Peloton in 2021. At that point, my team was probably around 12 people, and we were supporting 30+ product pods across software and hardware development, plus regularly fielding questions and requests from our wonderful partner teams - Content, Brand Marketing, Strategy, Investor Relations, PR, Community. 

The analysts were starting to get overwhelmed. The product analyst life is full enough of context-switching even without ad hocs - between defining taxonomy, designing experiments, doing impact calculations, and launch analyses.

On the other hand, as the team became larger and the product team started to operate in a pod model, our knowledge started to get more siloed - if someone was working on the digital growth pod, they knew everything about the in-app onboarding funnel but nobody else did.

Thanks for reading Dramatic Analyst! Subscribe for free to receive new posts in your inbox!

So I had an idea of picking a ‘point person’ who can field small requests on a given week while both allowing everyone else on the team to focus better, and for them to learn about subjects and stakeholders they normally don’t face. Together with my project manager (that role on my team was short-lived, it ended up not being as beneficial as I envisioned it) we interviewed some of our software engineering managers about their version of on-call, and I’d ‘cold’ reached out to the wonderful after seeing a mention of her giving a talk on leveraging an on-call system at Reddit. 

As a result, after a couple of collaborative sessions with our team and an 8-week pilot, we came up with the following system:

  • One person per week is on call with a time box of 10 hours (each person schedules as works for them - 2 hrs every day or two-three larger chunks), only during their regular work hours.

  • All requests (except for ‘where do I find X?’) would go through a form that required the requestor to articulate the ‘why’ behind the request and explain the dependencies if the desired deadline was really tight

    • Check out this great article about designing a great intake form!

  • The SLA for getting back on the request (not necessarily solving it fully) was 48 hours since we didn’t have any operational/production use cases in our scope

  • The on-call analyst would triage the requests (with my help, as needed) and determine if some requests were too big to be done in a couple of hours (e.g. require a net new deep research project). In this case we would pick the person on the team the most versed in the subject and have them have a more deep conversation around business impact, scope, and prioritize it on their roadmap as it allows.

  • The on-call analyst would also monitor our team slack channel for any ‘quick questions’ throughout the shift

  • At the end of the weekly shift, the on-call analyst would write a quick recap in the shared doc to highlight if some projects were unfinished and had to be picked up, or if they’ve noticed a specific emerging pattern in requests

This structure alleviated concerns about on-call completely overtaking folks’ agendas and making it hard for their product prods to rely on their support and made it much easier for analysts to anticipate when they would be more distracted, so they didn’t plan any meaty projects for their on-call weeks resulting in logging off on Friday with a disappointed feeling. 

We’d schedule shifts in advance using a survey where folks could pick which weeks they coudn’t be on call (because of PTO or workload), so we had a primary + emergency backup on-call schedule set for a couple months out.

Each couple of cycles, I would survey the team - asking them if the on-call workload was manageable, if they’d learned anything new, and if they were feeling more focused when not on-call, to make sure the system was still working.

Side effects… or primary benefits?

One of the benefits of this system that combined a low-friction way to submit a request without having to worry about immediate pushback with the centralized request logging, plus the built-in weekly reflections was that it became easier for us to spot important trends in requests.

And yes, as you would expect, 60%+ of requests were something that a data scientist would call ‘unhelpful’ (either not actionable/just curious or the question asked was not the right question to solve the underlying ‘why’). But, first of all, it is great that a lot of people are ‘just curious’ and it should be encouraged. And understanding the patterns of what people are curious about can lead to identifying our own blind spots.

 If many people asked us about ‘what song was the most played in this month’s playlists?’ in the last few weeks - was there some strategic conversation about music happening that we weren’t a part of? Was there some hypothesis around changing patterns of impact of music on engagement? At the very least, we would make sure we build and socialize dashboards where stakeholders can self-serve insights about different touchpoints with music and playlists at Peloton, but even better if it was the birth of a new impactful deep-dive analysis.

Strength in Numbers

Of course, if you have a much smaller team, a lot of benefits of this system are less prominent. Being on call every three weeks is very different from ‘every 2 months’. But it still helps create more focus for the teammates and learn new datasets and sets of problems. With a three-person team at Bubble, we are doing a much less formal version of this system - without an intake form (for now) and very rigid time limits, but as the team grows, I will look to refine it more to relive the old glory days :) 

Are you leveraging a similar system on your data team? How do you go about ad hoc requests?

item.title: The unbearable lightness of… naming things…
item.description: …or why Button Clicked won’t get you anywhere (or not too far anyways)
item.dc:creator: Elena Dyachkova
item.content:encoded:
I am generally a pretty indecisive and non-opinionated person, in most situations I can easily see and empathize with both sides and have a hard time taking one (analysis-paralysis, anyone?). But there is one thing that I am now pretty certain about. If you are working in product analytics, please don’t name your user interaction events ‘Page Viewed’ and ‘Button Clicked’.

The Proof is in the “Poking”

In one of my previous roles, as I joined the company and opened their product analytics tool, I saw that the vast majority of events were ‘Button Clicked’, ‘Page Viewed’, and ‘Form Submitted’, and thought: ‘This is going to be a journey!’. And I was not wrong. 

Within the first few days I heard from a product manager: ‘This product analytics tool sucks!’. Another person said: ‘I’m pretty sure the numbers in this tool are wrong’.

Of course, there was nothing wrong with the tool itself, and while numbers were indeed wrong in one specific part of the funnel, the rest of it was fine. The product managers just couldn’t use it because they couldn’t reliably and confidently select the right events to trend or to create funnels with.

I even did some live “user research” sessions when I asked product managers to open our existing tool and its slightly shinier competitor and plot one of the product’s key actions, while narrating their thought process. Now I could see for myself that the tool was indeed not the culprit. They were stumped between Button Clicked and Form Submitted, as well as, whichever of these events they picked, how to correctly apply additional filters to get to the required user action. Faced with this conundrum every time they tried to investigate some trend, they just gave up and chalked it up to the ‘tool’ not helping them enough, while really it was in their power all along to suggest a different naming.

Incentives, incentives

Why was it implemented that way? Because an engineer (an a brilliant one at that - one of my favorite engineers ever to work with, and one of the most knowledgeable about event tracking SDKs) built it in a way that optimized for an easy implementation on dev side as they didn’t have a data or a PM thought partner to develop a full-fledged taxonomy.

I recently asked my Twitter to chime in on their event naming preference, and ‘descriptive naming’ of the action won, but not unanimously. 

I expected it to be even closer, given that I follow some data engineering and ML crowd there (I guess, they don’t follow me back! 😅), as another argument I’ve heard “pro” generic naming was the ease of wrangling all the event data into a big ol’ ML model. Although if you think about it, that argument also falls apart fairly quickly. Once you get beyond some basic event properties like ‘type’, ‘page’, ‘source’, and start collecting some richer event metadata, you end up with a colander of a segment.button_clicked table in the warehouse, that has lots of columns and lots of them (all the properties specific to a handful of events) having lots of NULLs.

Where I was going with it anyways…

So, why descriptive naming? If you’ve worked with a product team, you know that the Voldermort-like concept of ‘self-serve analytics’ is not a privilege but a must. You, as a data person, really cannot be a bottleneck for the need to look up the adoption of a feature, pull a cohort of users who did X in the last Y days, or segment a funnel. 

Product managers and UX designers are curious people, their curiosity and exploration while they are in the flow of product development is something to be encouraged and enabled. They have to have the right systems in place for that, and the need to parse through a bunch of event tracking schema documentation (if it even exists, because who are we kidding) or the constant confusion of how many filters to apply to a generic event is the opposite of the right system.

User-centric taxonomy design

But, of course, there is no need to take the ‘descriptive naming’ to an extreme. My former colleague Gaurav, I think, got it right. 

For marketing websites and landing pages that primarily enable users navigate through content, Page Viewed, Link Clicked nomenclature is sufficient (for page views, in tools like Segment you can even leverage ‘page’ calls that come with a set of standard properties, just don’t forget to add a custom ‘name’ property, or your tracking plan will be blown up). 

But for the actual product surface with a more involved functionality, when you think about naming an event, think: ‘If John from the product marketing team, needs to see how many people shared their book reading badge to social, how would he start looking for it in Amplitude… he would probably start typing ‘shared…’... so we should name it Shared to Social - that way he won’t miss it’.

And we can add properties for what they shared (shared asset: ‘badge’/’new year’s resolution’), where they shared (destination: Facebook / Twitter), and which screen did the share happen from (source: user profile, challenge completion, home screen).

There is a different risk here - of getting too descriptive. Should this be ‘Shared Challenge Badge to Social’. Or even ‘Shared Challenge Badge to Facebook – Challenge Completion Screen’. But it is also pretty easy to think through this consideration: what is the most common way the data will be aggregated? Is the most common metric ‘% users sharing (anything) to social’? Or is it more common to look at challenge badges separately? It is generally much easier to ‘group by’ in product analytics tools than to ‘union’, so you should always go by the most common level of granularity.

All in all, it all boils down to the notion of carefully considering the end user of your data vs the skillset and resources of your data team. If you have more analytics engineer-type folks on your team and have tools and time to massage the raw event data before it makes it into your product analytics interface of choice, you can spend less time defining the taxonomy and QAing data with the eng team, otherwise - you will need to be more intentional and deliberate about your taxonomy (and don’t forget about event properties, as Josh Wills (former Head of Data Engineering at Slack) once said, the cheapest way to join the data is in production!). It may sound daunting, but it is a bit of a muscle to build with the team (plus, if you can swing it, there are some tools out there that can make things easier, although a spreadsheet works too).

If you’ve read all this way and still don’t think I’m totally off-base, I will be more than happy to share my ‘taxonomy guidelines’ template with you! Hit me up in the comments!
